assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks (magic-wavelength trapping proposed by Katori, then realised with strontium and developed to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18) are a textbook case of a measurement technique that moved the limit of what can be measured. They give redefinition-grade time standards, tests of fundamental-constant drift and relativistic geodesy, and they enable other work. This fits well with a view that progress is limited by how precisely we can measure.
assessment.attribution: Katori made the original magic-wavelength lattice proposal and early demonstrations. Ye's JILA group pushed the clock to its performance limits and made it a platform for many-body physics. Both names are in the supplied credit list, so a two-person prize is clean. The 2005 prize to Hall and Hansch covered the frequency comb, which is a separate enabling step, and I do not see an overlap problem.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Several independent groups (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others) have confirmed performance, and the redefinition of the second is being discussed. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: I am working from memory on exact uncertainty figures and on which group first reached each milestone.
Whether Lemonde, Lisdat, or ion-clock groups (Wineland already recognised) should share the credit is not settled by the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with cold atoms in optical lattices (Mott insulator transition, quantum gas microscopy, Hubbard-model simulation) created a new experimental way of observing many-body physics with single-site resolution and tunable parameters. It has opened a field, connects atomic physics to condensed matter, and is a genuine measurement and control achievement.
assessment.attribution: The theory proposal of Jaksch and Zoller, the Greiner/Bloch Mott-insulator experiment, and Bloch's and Greiner's microscopes are the decisive pieces; Esslinger's fermionic work is also strong. Choosing three from four credited names forces an uncomfortable exclusion (Esslinger, and Jaksch is not on the list). I propose Bloch, Greiner and Zoller as the most defensible three, with Esslinger a close alternative.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely reproduced by many groups for over two decades. Related cold-atom work was recognised in 2001 and 1997/2012, so the novelty of this specific step needs to be argued clearly, but the field's continued growth supports timing.
uncertainties: Allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger and Zoller is not clean.
Overlap with earlier BEC (2001) and cooling (1997) prizes may be seen as incremental by some.
Real quantum advantage from analogue simulation is still being established.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turned matter waves into a precision sensor for gravity, rotation, gravity gradients and the fine-structure constant, and for tests of equivalence principle. It is a clear instrument-driven advance that I would expect to matter increasingly for geodesy and navigation, which is a practical impact beyond physics.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard's group made the first atom interferometer with a grating/beam splitter, Bordé gave the theory of Ramsey-Bordé interferometry and the light-pulse scheme, and Kasevich and Chu demonstrated the light-pulse interferometer. Chu is not in the list, which weakens the fairness of any configuration. The three supplied names are still a defensible trio, though Chu's absence is a concern.
assessment.maturity: Mature techniques with several independent groups, but the most compelling applications (field-deployable gravimeters, equivalence-principle tests at 1e-12 or better) are still maturing. Recognition is reasonable though attribution is the limit.
uncertainties: Absence of Steven Chu in the credited names undermines the attribution picture.
Early historical priority between Pritchard, Mlynek, Helmcke and Bordé is contested and I cannot verify details.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED reached strong coupling between microwave photons and superconducting qubits and made the transmon and dispersive readout the standard architecture for superconducting quantum processors. It is a precise-measurement-and-control success that underlies a very large experimental effort.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Girvin and Schoelkopf (with Wallraff, Devoret) are the standard attribution, and Wallraff's 2004 experiment is not among the credited names, which leaves a hole. Among the supplied names Schoelkopf is the key experimentalist, Blais and Girvin the theory.
assessment.maturity: Highly confirmed and used by dozens of groups. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, so this is adjacent and arguably timely, but the committee would need to consider overlap and whether the field needs more time to show a clear device payoff.
uncertainties: Missing Wallraff and Devoret from the credited list complicates a fair configuration.
Overlap with the most recent circuit-based prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single NV centres in diamond gave a room-temperature solid-state quantum sensor with nanoscale magnetic and thermal sensitivity, with uses in materials, biology and quantum networks. The measurement angle is strong, and it is concrete and demonstrated.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko made the first single-NV optical detection and spin control; Lukin's group built extensively on it for sensing and quantum registers. Awschalom, Hanson and others also contributed, so the configuration is less settled than the supplied names suggest.
assessment.maturity: Substantial independent confirmation across many labs. Sensing applications are still moving toward robust devices, and the field is expanding, so recognition would be timely but possibly early for the sensing impact.
uncertainties: Allocation versus Awschalom, Hanson and Wrachtrup/Jelezko priority is debatable.
Practical sensitivity beyond established methods depends on application.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: EIT and slow light show that quantum interference can make an opaque medium transparent and slow light to a few metres per second, opening coherent control of light and quantum memory for light. I know this physics well from rare-earth crystals and I regard it as an enabling technique, although its direct measurement impact is narrower than clocks or interferometry.
assessment.attribution: Harris proposed and demonstrated EIT; Hau's slow-light experiment is the dramatic demonstration. Imamoglu contributed theory but I consider his role less decisive here. Two laureates are the clean choice. As a disclosure, my own research is in related slow-light and memory work, so I treat this with caution.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely replicated in gases, solids and fibres. Recognition would be late rather than premature, and the main question is whether this is a technique or a finished discovery.
uncertainties: Potential perceived bias from my own related work.
Hau's slow-light result depends on EIT, so the credit is hard to separate from Harris.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed-light injection improved the sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors beyond the shot-noise limit, which is a precision-measurement milestone in routine use. Caves' proposal made the quantum limits clear, and experiments by Kimble's group generated squeezed states, while Schnabel and GEO600 brought it to operation.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread across theory (Caves), early squeezing (Slusher, Kimble, Wu) and detector integration (Schnabel, GEO600, LIGO). The supplied names cover most but not all of it, and Slusher and Walls are missing.
assessment.maturity: Operationally confirmed at GEO600 and LIGO/Virgo, but the discovery of squeezing dates from the 1980s and the prize case would partly overlap with the 2017 LIGO prize.
uncertainties: Unclear whether it is a distinct discovery or an enabling detail of gravitational-wave detection.
Important contributors are missing from the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade and programmable tweezer arrays give flexible quantum simulators and processors with individually addressable atoms, and they allowed coherent control of dozens to hundreds of atoms. Experimentally impressive and fast moving.
assessment.attribution: Lukin proposed the Rydberg blockade with Jaksch and Zoller and led large array experiments; Browaeys and Saffman gave key demonstrations of blockade and arrays. Bloch and Endres, Thompson and others also contributed, so configuration is not yet clear.
assessment.maturity: Still maturing: reproducibility is good across several groups but error rates and scalability claims are being tested. Probably premature compared with the older candidates ranked above.
uncertainties: Premature because the field is developing quickly.
Credit is unsettled and overlaps with B010 and B014.
